# Data Processing

### Quadratic-smooth derivative difference

To calculate the difference between the smooth and quadratic derivatives, we can't simply sum their
uncertainties, because we need to account for their covariance.

We take a nonparametric bootstrap, meaning we sample from the actual data. Within each replicate, we
standardize the mean weight to 1, so that each replicate is equal in information, even if it happens
to have a lower total weight, because mgcv is sensitive to the scale of weights. We take samples
based on the primary sampling units within strata, rather than individuals. Within each replicate,
we fit a GAM and quadratic model to the same data, calculate the derivative for each age, and
subtract the quadratic derivative from the smooth to obtain a difference. If the sample at a given
age is randomly higher and this bump raises the GAM's derivative but drops the derivative of the
quadratic (if, for example, the bump leads to a higher intercept or linear component with lower
quadratic component to compensate, i.e., the derivative rotates), then there is negative covariance
and we get a higher total variance for that age. This means that both within-model variance and
across-model covariance is accounted for when we compute the standard error from the bootstrap.

The PSU-based sampling creates an interaction variable for PSU \* stratum, so that we identify the
PSUs within each stratum. We then identify the rows/IDs pertaining to each PSU. We then identify
which PSUs belong to which stratum. We then randomly sample PSUs within each stratum. For example,
if have 3 PSUs within one stratum, one bootstrap replicate we may have 1 2 3, another 1 1 3, another
2 2 2, another 1 3 1, etc. When a PSU is sampled, we include all rows/IDs within that PSU.
Individuals inside the same PSU are not independent, as they're from the same, for example,
geographical location. A single stratum may be, for example, high socioeconomic rural Texan black
females, and they might have 3 centers where this demographic is sampled. Each center is then a
single PSU. By sampling individuals, the model sees noise at a person level (sometimes a person is
duplicated, some are dropped), assuming people are independent, which they're not because people
within a PSU share geographical context, but with a PSU bootstrap, the model sees noise at the
cluster level. Some replicates a PSU with systematically more hearing loss gets sampled twice. The
bootstrapping then tells us the uncertainty based on 'what if this whole sampled cluster had more or
less influence' instead of 'what if these isolated people had more or less influence'. This mimics
'what if NHANES had sampled different PSUs' instead of 'what if NHANES had picked different people
from the same PSUs', which is less generalizable.

We correct the variance at the end, taking into account the number of PSUs per stratum. We then
correct the variance with $\frac{n}{(n-1)}$. This is needed because we sample with replacement, if
we have PSU A and B in a strata, we have 50% chance to draw AA or BB and 50% to draw AB or BA (the
original mean). The mean contribution is then about half the true sampling variance. If each stratum
had 2 PSUs, we could've multiplied by $\sqrt2$, but since some strata have 3 PSUs, we need to
calculate the harmonic mean.

Furthermore, we sample 1 point for each age and predict the PTA using the smooth-only model.

To calculate the quadratic derivative, we can either calculate the slope at each point manually with

`coef(m)["age"] + 2 * coef(m)["I(age^2)"] * seq(min(df$age), max(df$age), 1)}`

Or we use emtrends to calculate the slope at each point. The result is the same. We use
`derivatives()` from gratia to calculate the smooth derivative.

```{r}
predict_age_rate_bootstrap <- function(
    df,
    model,
    type = "predict",
    covariate = NULL,
    reference_model = NULL,
    n_boot = params$n_boot,
    threads = max(1, min(params$n_threads, availableCores() - 1))
) {
  # Get grid of all ages
  ages <- seq(
    min(df[["age"]], na.rm = TRUE),
    max(df[["age"]], na.rm = TRUE),
    by = 1
  )
  
  # Add covariates to the prediction grid if in the passed formula
  if (is.null(covariate)) {
    newdata <- data.frame(age = ages)
  } else {
    newdata <- expand.grid(
      age = ages,
      covariate_level = unique(df[[covariate]])
    )
    
    names(newdata) <- c("age", covariate)
  }
  
  model_formula <- formula(model)
  
  # Store reference model for the derivative difference only
  reference_formula <- if (!is.null(reference_model)) {
    formula(reference_model)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
  
  # Extract predictions or derivatives without using model-based SEs
  predict_model <- function(model, data) {
    if (type == "predict") {
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          model,
          newdata = newdata,
          type = "response"
        )
      )
    } else if (length(model$smooth) > 0) {
      derivatives(
        model,
        select = "s(age)",
        data = newdata
      ) %>%
        as.data.frame() %>%
        pull(.derivative)
    } else {
      as.data.frame(
        emtrends(
          model, ~age,
          var = "age",
          at = list(age = ages),
          data = data
        )
      )$age.trend
    }
  }
  
  predictions <- predict_model(model, df)
  
  # Get derivative differences
  if (!is.null(reference_model)) {
    predictions <- predictions - predict_model(reference_model, df)
  }
  
  # Store PSU rows for bootstrap
  psu_id <- interaction(df$stratum, df$psu, drop = TRUE)
  psu_rows <- split(seq_len(nrow(df)), psu_id, drop = TRUE)
  stratum_psus <- split(names(psu_rows), df$stratum[match(names(psu_rows), as.character(psu_id))])
  
  set.seed(2)
  plan(multisession, workers = threads)
  
  bootstrap_predictions <- simplify2array(future_lapply(
    seq_len(n_boot),
    function(i) {
      indices <- unlist(lapply(stratum_psus, function(psus) {
        unlist(psu_rows[sample(psus, replace = TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)
      }), use.names = FALSE)
      
      data_subset <- df[indices, ]
      
      # Fit with sample weights
      fit <- function(model_formula) {
        bam(
          model_formula,
          data = data_subset,
          weights = weights / mean(weights),
          method = "REML",
          family = gaussian()
        )
      }
      
      pred <- predict_model(
        fit(model_formula),
        data_subset
      )
      
      # Fit the reference to the same sample and calculate a paired difference
      if (!is.null(reference_formula)) {
        pred <- pred - predict_model(
          fit(reference_formula),
          data_subset
        )
      }
      
      pred
    },
    future.seed = TRUE,
    future.globals = TRUE,
    future.packages = c(
      "emmeans",
      "mgcv",
      "tidytable",
      "gratia"
    )
  ))
  
  plan(sequential)
  
  SE_adj <- apply(bootstrap_predictions, 1, sd)
  
  # Get simultaneous intervals
    t_crit_max_t <- unname(quantile(
      apply(
        abs(sweep(bootstrap_predictions, 1, rowMeans(bootstrap_predictions), "-") / SE_adj),
        2,
        max
      ),
      0.95
    ))
  
  # Apply the stratum correction (strata have length 2 or 3)
  SE_adj <- SE_adj / sqrt(1 - mean(1 / lengths(stratum_psus)))
  
  predictions <- newdata %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(
      estimate = predictions,
      SE = SE_adj,
      ci_lower = estimate - t_crit_max_t * SE,
      ci_upper = estimate + t_crit_max_t * SE
    )
  
  if (!is.null(reference_model)) {
    predictions %>%
      transmute(
        derivative_adj = estimate,
        SE_adj = SE,
        t_crit_max_t = t_crit_max_t,
        ci_lower_adj = ci_lower,
        ci_upper_adj = ci_upper
      )
  } else if (type == "predict_derivative") {
    predictions %>%
      rename(derivative = estimate)
  } else {
    predictions
  }
  }

# Main age-rate curves and derivatives
pred_age_rate <- list()

system.time(
  pred_age_rate <- append(
    pred_age_rate,
    list(
      linear = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$linear,
        type = "predict"
      ),
      linear_derivative = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$linear,
        type = "predict_derivative"
      ),
      quadratic = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$quadratic,
        type = "predict"
      ),
      quadratic_derivative = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$quadratic,
        type = "predict_derivative"
      ),
      smooth = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$smooth,
        type = "predict"
      ),
      derivative_smooth = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_age_rate$smooth,
        type = "predict_derivative"
      )
    )
  )
)

# Smooth-minus-quadratic derivative difference
system.time(
  pred_age_rate$derivative_smooth <- cbind(
    pred_age_rate$derivative_smooth,
    predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
      df,
      models_age_rate$smooth,
      type = "predict_derivative",
      reference_model = models_age_rate$quadratic
    )
  )
)

# Covariate curves
pred_covariates_full <- list()

system.time(
  pred_covariates_full <- append(
    pred_covariates_full,
    list(
      smooth_sex = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_covariates$smooth_sex,
        covariate = "sex"
      ),
      smooth_smoking = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_covariates$smooth_smoking,
        covariate = "smoking"
      ),
      smooth_race = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_covariates$smooth_race,
        covariate = "race"
      ),
      smooth_education = predict_age_rate_bootstrap(
        df,
        models_covariates$smooth_education,
        covariate = "education"
      )
    )
  )
)
```

The confidence intervals of the smooth curve wiggle considerably. Diagnostic tests (not shown)
revealed that these oscillations are the result of variation in the smoothing parameter calculated
over different bootstrap samples. The overall curve remains the same but the local slope (i.e., a
point on the derivative) can differ quite a bit. Small perturbations to the dataset can produce
considerable deviations in the local slope. Uncertainty in the smoothing parameter is a real
component of generalized additive models and should not be ignored. The gratia package, for example,
calculates confidence intervals with a fixed smoothing parameter, but that is not per se justified.
In our case, we have 4.7 effective degrees of freedom in the full dataset fit, whereas the median of
the bootstrap is 5.47. This uncertainty in the amount of small, local wiggliness is real and
important for hypothesis testing. If we would consider the smoothing parameter fixed/certain, we
could wrongly interpret a hump in the derivative as significant when that hump is actually
'incidental', many small local slopes after all can produce very similar complete curves. A straight
line up vs a wavy line up that only wiggles minutely would have completely different local slopes
even if the global slope is the same, and thus if we ask whether there are specific ages during
which the rate of hearing loss speeds up/slows down must consider that uncertainty.
